video_title: Philip & Allan Maymin – Compounding Through Risk, Not Return (S7E35)
gist: Philip and Allan Maymin of Janus Henderson (founded by Myron Scholes) argue that compounding is improved more reliably by managing risk than by chasing return, using option-implied upside and downside tail signals across thousands of assets within a client drawdown budget. They also explain why the 60/40 benchmark, tail correlation heuristics and simple explainable models underpin the process.

insights.claim: Compound growth equals average return minus a risk penalty, so for any positive alpha there is a risk level at which the investor goes bankrupt; the two can report a stable 5% average return while the investor is wiped out. Maximizing arithmetic average return while ignoring path dependency is the core mistake.
insights.speaker: Phil Maymin, co-head of global asset allocation, Janus Henderson
insights.so_what: Judge funds on compounded outcomes and drawdown, not average return or Sharpe-style averages.

insights.claim: Risk is a more controllable lever than return for improving compounding because alpha is hard to measure and unstable, whereas risk estimates sharpen with finer data frequency.
insights.speaker: Phil Maymin, co-head of global asset allocation, Janus Henderson
insights.so_what: Favors durable risk-management edges over alpha-hunting that decays when regimes shift.

insights.claim: Per Merton's 1980 appendix, statistically distinguishing a mean return from zero depends only on total sample length, not data frequency, so it can take decades; variance can be estimated precisely by slicing returns finer (monthly to daily to hourly).
insights.speaker: Phil Maymin, co-head of global asset allocation, Janus Henderson
insights.so_what: Short track records say little about alpha, but say a lot about risk.

insights.claim: The Maymins argue the 'middle-income world' of average-return thinking is misleading: a series where 99% of paths fail and 1% succeed hugely can show a good average. Investors should set goals, set a tolerable drawdown, then maximize compounded rate of return.
insights.speaker: Phil Maymin, co-head of global asset allocation, Janus Henderson
insights.so_what: Reframes portfolio objectives around terminal wealth for a specific client path.

insights.claim: 60/40 is effectively a proxy for a ~30% drawdown tolerance: equities fall ~50% in turmoil, and 60% equity with uncorrelated bonds gives roughly 30%. Once drawdown is the explicit objective, there is no reason to rely on a static mix or on bonds as a hedge.
insights.speaker: Phil Maymin, co-head of global asset allocation, Janus Henderson
insights.so_what: Question the 60/40 benchmark's provenance; a drawdown budget can be met dynamically.

insights.claim: Stock-bond negative correlation was a multi-decade anomaly; over the last 100-150 years they were mostly positively correlated, which is logical since both carry large expected positive returns. 2022 showed both can lose at once.
insights.speaker: Phil Maymin, co-head of global asset allocation, Janus Henderson
insights.so_what: Bond diversification of equity drawdowns should not be assumed in portfolio construction.

insights.claim: Portfolio construction is hierarchical: step one sets total equity-vs-cash exposure from the remaining drawdown budget (budget used lowers risk taken); step two optimizes fixed income and other assets while staying close to the step-one path; later steps handle constraints, regional sleeves and trading costs.
insights.speaker: Allan Maymin, co-head of global asset allocation, Janus Henderson
insights.so_what: Most risk is the equity/cash decision; the rest is deliberately constrained to avoid optimizer overfitting.

insights.claim: Passive dollar allocation is not passive in risk terms: risk varies sharply by month and regime, so some periods contribute disproportionate portfolio risk. Time-series risk concentration deserves the same attention as cross-sectional concentration.
insights.speaker: Phil Maymin, co-head of global asset allocation, Janus Henderson
insights.so_what: Supports volatility-targeting over static weights.

insights.claim: The process reads upside and downside tail risk from options (about the 10-delta / 90th-percentile strikes) and optimizes the ratio of expected tail gain to expected tail loss (CVaR90 over CVaR10). It treats the middle of the distribution as noise, claiming one can drop the middle 80% and retain essentially the same risk.
insights.speaker: Phil Maymin, co-head of global asset allocation, Janus Henderson
insights.so_what: The edge is tail asymmetry across thousands of assets, rather than expected-return forecasts.

insights.claim: The risk-neutral vs real-world (Q vs P) gap is mostly drift, and distribution shape is robust to the measure change; the signal uses changes in tail shape relative to an asset's own history and peers, so P vs Q is not a major concern.
insights.speaker: Phil Maymin, co-head of global asset allocation, Janus Henderson
insights.so_what: Defends using option-implied distributions as real-world risk signals.

insights.claim: Implied volatility subsumes realized volatility in forecasting: regressing future volatility on both gives full weight to implied and none to realized. The Maymins say the same holds for implied tail gains and losses, and they claim to have done research supporting it.
insights.speaker: Phil Maymin, co-head of global asset allocation, Janus Henderson
insights.so_what: Option-implied inputs are the best available forward-looking risk predictor.

insights.claim: They deliberately use 2-3 month options to match their risk horizon and focus on price/volatility changes rather than volume. Surging zero-day option volume from retail 'lottery ticket' buying, absorbed by delta-hedging market makers, carries little information, though short tenors may suit stat-arb.
insights.speaker: Allan Maymin, co-head of global asset allocation, Janus Henderson
insights.so_what: Don't read 0DTE volume as informative sentiment on a multi-month horizon.

insights.claim: Options aggregate the confidence-weighted views of thousands of analysts, like a prediction market. The Maymins say they don't believe options are mispriced and use them like GPS traffic data; deviating is possible but ignoring them forfeits information on unknown unknowns.
insights.speaker: Phil Maymin, co-head of global asset allocation, Janus Henderson
insights.so_what: Treat option prices as free consensus information, not as a trade target.

insights.claim: Correlations are unstable in the middle of distributions (stock-bond moving from -0.3 to +0.3) but tend toward one in the tails, so the problem reduces to choosing +1 or -1. Tail correlation is inferred from each asset's current implied-vol percentile: both high implies +1, one high and one low implies -1, both mid implies about 0.
insights.speaker: Allan Maymin, co-head of global asset allocation, Janus Henderson
insights.so_what: A cheap, regime-based heuristic for tail correlation that avoids estimating full covariance.

insights.claim: LTCM's lessons: correlations go to unity in the tails, and rumors alone can widen spreads because others believe you hold a position. This led to the view that arbitrage is self-limiting in the tails and sometimes it is better not to scale even when you can.
insights.speaker: Phil Maymin, co-head of global asset allocation, Janus Henderson
insights.so_what: Crowded or rumored positions carry reflexive risk beyond own holdings.

insights.claim: The signal-to-noise ratio is low and there is only one historical path, so they require an economic rationale for any signal and the simplest expression of it. Explainability lets one stay with a temporarily underperforming strategy at longer horizons; the 'faster = dumber' quip is reframed as explained versus unexplained.
insights.speaker: Allan Maymin, co-head of global asset allocation, Janus Henderson
insights.so_what: Guards against overfitting; patience requires a story, not just a backtest.

insights.claim: Many HFT and stat-arb strategies work better in crashes because they profit from forced, uninformed mechanical flow (delta hedging, ETF day trading); in the 2010 flash crash a market maker made a risky bet in an illiquid market.
insights.speaker: Allan Maymin, co-head of global asset allocation, Janus Henderson
insights.so_what: Crash flows reward liquidity providers; the loop is self-reinforcing.

insights.claim: Volatility time: since Black-Scholes model depends only on sigma times root-T, a 'risk day' can pass in an hour during stress (e.g., COVID) or take days in calm. A systematic process lets one prepare during lulls and execute under stress without cognitive biases.
insights.speaker: Phil Maymin, co-head of global asset allocation, Janus Henderson
insights.so_what: Argues for pre-committed rules given compressed decision time in crises.

insights.claim: Dynamic risk management is not crowded because large allocators are benchmark-constrained and mechanically rebalance. Scholes' vision is that dynamic, risk-managed benchmarks become the norm, and he welcomes the edge being competed away, like everyone using a traffic-aware GPS.
insights.speaker: Phil Maymin, co-head of global asset allocation, Janus Henderson
insights.so_what: The edge relies on institutional constraints; widespread adoption would be the signal it has faded.

insights.claim: Clients increasingly want after-tax goals, so the optimizer treats taxes as inputs: prefer selling tax-loss lots, defer short-term to long-term gains. 'Locked-in' portfolios after long rallies are mitigated by long/short use and by paying taxes when position risk justifies it.
insights.speaker: Phil Maymin, co-head of global asset allocation, Janus Henderson
insights.so_what: Tax-aware customized risk management is a growing demand.
